title: hetero-expert-scheduling-latency-diagnostics
content:
Summary:

This note captures an ad-hoc investigation into end-to-end latency variance we observed running MoE-enabled long-context workloads across heterogeneous GPU pools (A100/H100 mixed). The problem manifests as intermittent 2–6x tail latency spikes when serving Llama/Mistral/Qwen MoE variants with context lengths >= 16k and mixed batch sizes. The goal here is to document hypotheses, lightweight profile snapshots, mitigation experiments we've tried, and a prioritized list of next steps.

Why this doc exists (short):
- Recent customer workload (large-chat app) hit transient tail latencies during peak load.
- Traces pointed to dispatch/routing and KV cache interaction as likely culprits; additional noise from memcpy/sync on heterogeneous devices.
- Need practical mitigations that can be staged in Dedicated and Private deployments.

Experiment setup (replicable):
- Models tested: Llama-2-13B-MoE (8 experts), Mistral-7B-MoE-4x (mock MoE), Qwen-14B-MoE (16 experts simulated routing).
- Hardware: mixed pool with 1x H100 80GB + 3x A100 40GB; CUDA 12.1, cuBLAS/cuDNN latest pinned at time of test, torch 2.2 nightly build used for micro-benchmarks.
- Requests: synthetic long-context continuation workload, prompt lengths 8k/16k/32k tokens; per-request generation 512 tokens; 99th percentile latency measured over 1 hour load test with Poisson arrivals (lambda scaled to target 80% util).
- Serving runtime flags: dynamic batching ON (max batch 16), async dispatch ON, KV cache prefix caching OFF for baseline, routing prefetch OFF for baseline.

High-level observations (quantified):
- Baseline 95th p: ~120 ms for non-MoE Llama 13B on H100 at 16k context. MoE variants baseline 95th p: ~200–300 ms, 99th p: 600–1800 ms depending on expert activation variance.
- Tail spikes correlate with: (A) sudden burst of new prefixes (cache miss paths), (B) expert-hotspot events (one expert selected by >60% of active tokens), (C) cross-device GPU-to-GPU memcpy for dispatch/collect when routing top-k experts span devices.
- Micro-profiling (sampling traces and flamegraphs): GEMM kernels ~40–55% of compute time in steady-state; dispatch/unsqueeze + memcpy + async-synchronization accounted for an unexpectedly large fraction of tail: memcpy/device-sync ~18–32% during spikes, kernel launch overhead and mutex contention ~10–16%.

Detailed findings and surprising failure modes:
1) Heterogeneous-device dispatch fragmentation:
   - When a single request's activated experts are split across H100/A100, we observed synchronous barriers waiting for the slower device (usually A100 on heavy FP16 GEMMs due to memory bandwidth/fragmentation). This is exacerbated by our current dispatcher calling per-expert CUDA streams in a sequence rather than fully pipelining.

2) Routing hot-experts + KV replay amplification:
   - Hot experts produce imbalanced work; if a hot expert is remote (different GPU), the extra memcpy/collect overhead is repeated per-token for long contexts. With long-contexts, the cost is additive across many KV lookups.

3) Small-op overhead dominates when experts are thin:
   - For MoE variants where experts are relatively small MLP subnets, we see GEMM times shrink but kernel launch + memcpy + enqueue cost becomes dominant. This explains why total latency doesn't proportionally decrease with smaller experts.

4) KV cache eviction/rehydration th undance:
   - Prefix cache misses cause sudden heavy-memory copies to reconstruct KV states. When many concurrent streams rehydrate KV for long prefixes, memory bandwidth contention and host<->device copies spike.

Mitigations tested (quick, with results):
A) Expert co-location scheduling (locality-first): pin likely-coactivated experts to the same GPU pool.
   - Effect: reduced cross-device memcpy by ~70% on those traces; 99th p latency dropped ~2.1x for workloads where routing distribution is steady.
   - Cost: reduces flexibility in capacity planning; needs placement reconciler for autoscaler.

B) Prefetch + async KV warmup for predicted prefixes:
   - Use a lightweight LRU of recent prefixes + background prefetch before request completion.
   - Effect: cut KV rehydration spikes by ~60% in synthetic repeating-prompt tests; not perfect for highly unique prompts.

C) Batch-aware routing smoothing (softmax temperature and top-k dampening):
   - Slightly increase softmax temperature in router and cap top-k per request to reduce identical-hot expert concentration.
   - Effect: reduced extreme expert hotness, smoothed per-request compute distribution, 99th p improved modestly (~15–25%). Potential slight model-quality impact (needs eval).

D) Fuse dispatch+collect kernels (experimental fused-op in PR):
   - Local microkernel that does routing index gather + fused memcpy into contiguous dispatch buffers on-device to avoid host scatter/gather.
   - Effect: synthetic microbench shows dispatch time reduced ~3–5x; integrated test reduced tail by ~30% where dispatch dominated.
   - Risk: engineering cost and cross-model correctness verification required.

E) Prefer H100 for long-context MoE (heuristic):
   - Assign long-context or high-KV workloads to H100-only workers when available.
   - Effect: improved stability; 95/99th p improved but overall utilization decreases on A100.

Measurement artifacts to be careful of:
- Sampling profiler underestimates small-kernel overhead; need a full CUDA tracing run (nvprof / Nsight) to capture kernel launch and memcpy timings accurately.
- Host-side synchronization in Python wrapper added ~5–10% extra latency during some runs; C++ path measurements were cleaner.
- Mixed-precision differences across GPUs: A100 FP16 math reductions produced different per-op timings vs H100 BF16 paths.

Recommendations (prioritized):
1) Immediate (low-effort, high-impact):
   - Implement expert-locality placement heuristic in scheduler (place top-expected experts on same device when request-level routing predictability exists). Track via routing frequency counters. (Owner: Diego Ramos, JIRA: SERV-1187)
   - Add KV prefetch knob at route-level for Dedicated customers with long-context SLAs (configurable TTL).

2) Medium-term (require engineering):
   - Prototype fused dispatch+collect kernels upstream (PR in flight: see linked PR). If fused op reduces dispatch overhead at scale, move to A/B test on Dedicated.
   - Add dynamic route smoothing option to the runtime that can be toggled per-deployment to reduce hot-expert concentration; expose metric for quality/regression evaluation.

3) Long-term / research:
   - Investigate routing-aware compilation: when model is compiled for a deployment, annotate experts and produce kernels that optimize for common activation patterns (inlined dispatch for the most common expert sets).
   - Evaluate alternative MoE routing algorithms (hash-based, clustering-based) that may trade a small quality delta for much stronger runtime regularity.

Next experiments (concrete):
- Run Nsight end-to-end on a failing trace to capture exact memcpy + kernel launch timeline (Ticket: SERV-1189).
- A/B deploy expert co-location for a subset of Dedicated customers and collect per-request routing histograms + end-to-end latency.
- Run synthetic long-tail test with routing smoothing enabled and run automated eval to measure quality drift on 10 evaluation prompts.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How often does routing distribution change over time for real workloads (minutes vs hours)? That affects how aggressive co-location can be without hurting cache hit ratios.
- Is there customer-tolerable quality loss for small smoothing of router softmax? Need product/CS input.
- Cost of fused-op maintenance across different model architectures (Llama style vs Mistral vs Qwen) — how much infra divergence will this create?

Appendix: quick trace sample (human-readable summary)
- Request ID: rq-20241015-1932 - Model: Llama-2-13B-MoE
- Context: 16,384 tokens, gen 512 tokens, batch size: 8
- Timeline (approx): enqueue -> route compute (CPU) 6 ms -> gather route indices 3 ms -> host->device memcpy dispatch buffers 28 ms -> expert GEMMs (distributed) 160 ms -> device->host collect + sync 42 ms -> kv rehydrate (if miss) 36 ms -> final decode kernels 18 ms -> total observed p99: 453 ms but spikes to 1.2s during hot-expert events.
